dossiers.title: The English says something materially different
dossiers.claim: George Henry Shaft repeatedly replaces the source proposition with a different action, state, object, or implication.
dossiers.sourcePattern: A locally recoverable Japanese proposition whose core content can be checked without relying on interpretive preference.
dossiers.georgeHenryShaftEffect: The English changes what happened or what was asserted, rather than merely choosing a different style.
dossiers.limits: This dossier includes only adjudicated changes of meaning. Loose but defensible paraphrase is not counted.
dossiers.diagnostic: 2,750 confirmed findings: 232 critical, 1,438 major, 973 moderate, 107 minor.

examples.japanese: 早朝だ。
examples.ghs: It's mid-morning.
examples.note: 早朝 explicitly means early morning. The English says 'mid-morning,' contradicting the stated time.

examples.japanese: 「なっ、君は、君というヤツは……それでも科学者か！」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "But! You... the person you are... you are still a scientist!"
examples.note: それでも科学者か challenges whether she can still call herself a scientist. The English instead affirms that she remains one.

examples.japanese: 『姪がさー、やっぱ群青行くんだけどさ、いろいろ教えてやらんと』
examples.ghs: Shinkawa: 『Got a niece, ya know, 'course she goes to Gunjou, ya know, so she's telling me lots and lots of stuff.』
examples.note: Shinkawa says his niece will also attend Gunjō and that he needs to teach her various things. The English says she already attends and reverses the teaching direction so that she tells him things.

examples.japanese: 押し黙る。
examples.ghs: She keeps silent.
examples.note: The Japanese says Taichi falls silent in response to Youko. The English assigns the silence to Youko.

examples.japanese: 「……人間じゃないですか」
examples.ghs: Kiri: "...are you not human?"
examples.note: Kiri protests that the supposedly wild beasts are human beings. The English instead asks whether Taichi himself is human.

examples.japanese: 「いっそ楽にしてくれよ～っと♪」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "Please release me from my pleee～asure!♪"
examples.note: 楽にしてくれ asks to be put out of his misery or relieved of suffering. The English chooses 'pleasure,' reversing pain relief into release from enjoyment.

examples.japanese: これは耳拷問、無意味に略せばみみごーではないか。
examples.ghs: this is Ear Torture, or if one wants to nonsensically abbreviate it, ExtraTerrestrial.
examples.note: The narrator nonsensically abbreviates 耳拷問, 'ear torture,' as みみごー to set up the following sound play. 'Extraterrestrial' has no relation to either component and replaces the joke with unrelated content.

examples.japanese: 部屋の生ぬるさが戻り、じんわりと身を包む。
examples.ghs: The room returning to half-hearted lukewarmth, I begin to dress myself.
examples.note: The lukewarm air of the room returns and gently envelops his body. The English calls the warmth 'half-hearted' and changes the room's enveloping action into Taichi beginning to dress himself.

dossiers.title: Causality and logical relations are reversed or blurred
dossiers.claim: Connectives, conditions, causes, contrasts, and consequences are repeatedly projected with the wrong relationship.
dossiers.sourcePattern: Japanese clauses whose relation is carried by an explicit connective, conditional form, or recoverable discourse structure.
dossiers.georgeHenryShaftEffect: The English can reverse agency or causality, or turn a qualification into a conclusion.
dossiers.limits: Only relations supported by the local syntax and context are included; genuinely open discourse links are excluded.
dossiers.diagnostic: 901 confirmed findings: 66 critical, 418 major, 353 moderate, 64 minor.

examples.japanese: 「そーとーストレスかかってるみたいだ」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "She seems to be taking in adequate amounts of stress."
examples.note: 相当ストレスかかってる says she is under considerable stress. 'Taking in adequate amounts of stress' makes stress an intake meeting a sufficient quota.

examples.japanese: 「なっ、君は、君というヤツは……それでも科学者か！」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "But! You... the person you are... you are still a scientist!"
examples.note: それでも科学者か challenges whether she can still call herself a scientist. The English instead affirms that she remains one.

examples.japanese: このガキ、空気を読むということをしないのか。
examples.ghs: Can't this ghoul of a brat just not read the mood?
examples.note: Taichi asks whether the brat cannot read the room. The English adds 'ghoul' and its double negative instead asks whether he can refrain from reading it.

examples.japanese: 「……合宿……つまらなかったな」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "...that training camp... wasn't that pointless."
examples.note: つまらなかった says the camp was boring, dull, or worthless. The English inserts negation and turns the judgment into its opposite.

examples.japanese: 「心の中でいろいろありまして、食う方に流れたわけだ」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "There's many things inside of the heart, and they flow there based on the ways you eat."
examples.note: Taichi says that various things happened in his heart and he consequently came down on the side of eating. The English makes plural things flow somewhere according to methods of eating.

examples.japanese: こんな悲しいことがあるだろうか。
examples.ghs: Is this sorrowful thing the truth then?
examples.note: The narrator asks whether anything could be sadder than this. The English instead asks whether an unspecified sad thing is true.

examples.japanese: 「……うう、わたしの身につけているものくらいしかお売り出来ないですね」
examples.ghs: Miki: "...ngh, and it's impossible to sell something that I've already worn, isn't it."
examples.note: Miki says that all she could sell would be what she is currently wearing. The English says that selling something already worn is impossible, reversing the proposition.

examples.japanese: 冬子を突き放したのだろう。
examples.ghs: To get away from Touko, that's why.
examples.note: Together with the preceding line, this asks why he had pushed Touko away. The English turns the second half into the answer 'To get away from Touko, that's why.'

dossiers.title: The actor or experiencer is assigned to the wrong person
dossiers.claim: Dropped Japanese subjects are repeatedly resolved to an English subject contradicted by the sentence or scene.
dossiers.sourcePattern: Subjectless or elliptical Japanese whose actor or experiencer is recoverable from grammar, continuity, or the immediately surrounding action.
dossiers.georgeHenryShaftEffect: Actions, perceptions, and responsibility move from one participant to another.
dossiers.limits: Ambiguous subject recovery is withheld; this dossier contains only source-bound assignments.
dossiers.diagnostic: 849 confirmed findings: 87 critical, 440 major, 257 moderate, 65 minor.

examples.japanese: 「……まあ、おまえたちの問題だと思うけど……正直、おまえの手が借りられないのはきつい」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "...well, it's only a problem between you guys, but... honestly, not even wanting your help, that's harsh."
examples.note: The speaker says that although it is the siblings' problem, not being able to borrow Tomoki's help is hard. 'Not even wanting your help' makes the speaker refuse assistance and reverses the relation.

examples.japanese: 『姪がさー、やっぱ群青行くんだけどさ、いろいろ教えてやらんと』
examples.ghs: Shinkawa: 『Got a niece, ya know, 'course she goes to Gunjou, ya know, so she's telling me lots and lots of stuff.』
examples.note: Shinkawa says his niece will also attend Gunjō and that he needs to teach her various things. The English says she already attends and reverses the teaching direction so that she tells him things.

examples.japanese: 押し黙る。
examples.ghs: She keeps silent.
examples.note: The Japanese says Taichi falls silent in response to Youko. The English assigns the silence to Youko.

examples.japanese: 「……人間じゃないですか」
examples.ghs: Kiri: "...are you not human?"
examples.note: Kiri protests that the supposedly wild beasts are human beings. The English instead asks whether Taichi himself is human.

examples.japanese: 「しようとしたけど、きついこと言われて引き下がった」
examples.ghs: Miki: "You were going to, but you were told something harsh and were stopped."
examples.note: Taichi admits in the first person that he tried but backed down after being told something harsh. The English labels Miki as speaker and changes the confession into her second-person account of his behavior.

examples.japanese: 部屋の生ぬるさが戻り、じんわりと身を包む。
examples.ghs: The room returning to half-hearted lukewarmth, I begin to dress myself.
examples.note: The lukewarm air of the room returns and gently envelops his body. The English calls the warmth 'half-hearted' and changes the room's enveloping action into Taichi beginning to dress himself.

examples.japanese: 「こんなとき美希ちんだったら、ぺろぺろと舐めて癒してくれるのに」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "If it was Miki-chan in this situation, you'll be healing her by going all licky-licky with your tongue wouldn't you!"
examples.note: Taichi says that if Miki were here, she would lick his wound better. The English leaves the nickname suffix unexplained and instead says Kiri will heal Miki, reversing healer and patient.

examples.japanese: 先輩を信じるのだ。
examples.ghs: Senpai believes it.
examples.note: The narrator exhorts himself to trust his senior. The English instead makes the senior the person who believes something and leaves the title untranslated.

dossiers.title: Meaning-bearing source material disappears
dossiers.claim: Words or clauses that materially constrain the sentence are repeatedly absent from the English.
dossiers.sourcePattern: Explicit Japanese content that contributes an object, modifier, relation, action, or rhetorical beat.
dossiers.georgeHenryShaftEffect: The English becomes less specific or loses part of the event, joke, or argument.
dossiers.limits: Routine compression is not counted unless it removes information needed to preserve the source meaning.
dossiers.diagnostic: 247 confirmed findings: 15 critical, 105 major, 74 moderate, 53 minor.

examples.japanese: 沖縄料理風の悲鳴を発し、俺は実をよじる。
examples.ghs: Emitting the name of the pig's ear dish in Okinawan cuisine in a literally ear-piercing scream, I make pun of the truth in ways untranslatable.
examples.note: The narrator emits 'Mimigaa,' evoking the Okinawan pig-ear dish mimigā, and writhes. The English converts the narration into translator commentary about untranslatability and omits the physical action entirely.

examples.japanese: マイケルのように、整形しろとでも。
examples.ghs: Like Michael, there's still plastic surgery, but...
examples.note: Taichi asks rhetorically whether he is expected to get plastic surgery like Michael. The English turns that challenge into a statement that surgery remains available and omits the implied demand.

examples.japanese: 缶は飛ばない。誰かが投げた。誰が？　今考える必要はない。投げる。意図。意図を持って投げた。目的は？　缶を投げることによって期待できる効果。投げた缶が効果を発揮。
examples.ghs: Cans do not fly. Somebody threw it.
examples.note: After noting that cans do not fly and someone threw them, the Japanese continues through a rapid chain of questions about actor, intent, purpose, and expected effect. The English omits nearly the entire unit.

examples.japanese: 支倉のかわりに入ってきたのは、新興の人物とその親類縁者だった。
examples.ghs:
Instead of the Hasekuras, new relatives that
were on the rise settled in.
examples.note: An upstart or newly wealthy man and his relatives replace the Hasekuras. The English omits the central man and says only that new relatives settled in.

examples.japanese: 「そうです。何も起こらなければ、ここは……」
examples.ghs: Misato: "Right then. If nothing goes wrong, because us being here..."
examples.note: The Japanese begins a conditional statement that if nothing had happened, this place or project would have proceeded. The English inserts 'because,' uses an object pronoun as a subject, and fails to convey the clause.

examples.japanese: 美希がどの程度の戦力を持っているかを調べる。第一に設定されるシークエンスだ。
examples.ghs:
However, Miki's threat level is an unknown
variable, and therefore caution was required.
examples.note: The Japanese describes investigating the extent of Miki's fighting strength as the first planned sequence. The English replaces the investigation and ordering with a generic warning about caution.

examples.japanese: 「もうちょっと」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "Seriously, look at this now!"
examples.note: While holding Misato, Taichi says 'a little longer.' The English replaces that duration with an unrelated command to look at something.

examples.japanese: 「……適応試験でやっちゃって……」
examples.ghs: Yusa: "...then I had the Conformity Test..."
examples.note: やっちゃって implies that something went badly on the aptitude or placement test. “Then I had the Conformity Test” merely states that she took it and omits the failure or mishap.

dossiers.title: The English adds unsupported content
dossiers.claim: George Henry Shaft repeatedly supplies actions, motives, descriptions, or relations not licensed by the Japanese.
dossiers.sourcePattern: A bounded source line whose asserted content can be compared directly with the added English material.
dossiers.georgeHenryShaftEffect: The translation invents facts or emphasis and can redirect characterization or scene logic.
dossiers.limits: Necessary English subjects and ordinary grammatical completion are not additions by themselves.
dossiers.diagnostic: 692 confirmed findings: 28 critical, 218 major, 266 moderate, 180 minor.

examples.japanese: 「柿の種にピーナッツ入っているものがある。知っているな」
examples.ghs: Sakuraba: "There is a type of seed of persimmon, or Kaki no Tane, that is actually a peanut-based snack usually served with beer. Did you know?"
examples.note: Sakuraba says some versions of the kaki no tane snack contain peanuts and asks whether they know that. The English describes a persimmon seed as a peanut-based snack and adds an unsolicited serving custom.

examples.japanese: これは耳拷問、無意味に略せばみみごーではないか。
examples.ghs: this is Ear Torture, or if one wants to nonsensically abbreviate it, ExtraTerrestrial.
examples.note: The narrator nonsensically abbreviates 耳拷問, 'ear torture,' as みみごー to set up the following sound play. 'Extraterrestrial' has no relation to either component and replaces the joke with unrelated content.

examples.japanese: 「これが俺のアイデンティティなんだよ。他の接し方はない」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "This is my eye-dentity indeed. Other ways to deal with things I haven't."
examples.note: アイデンティティ is simply the loanword 'identity.' The English invents an 'eye-dentity' pun absent from the source, then leaves the following sentence in non-English object-first order.

examples.japanese: 「そしていずれは、酸いも甘いも噛み分けたヤングアダルトへと変態していくのです」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "And then shall I, at last, pervert my awful nature into that of a Young Adult that is experienced in the ways of the world, having tasted its bitter and its sweet!"
examples.note: 変態する means transform or metamorphose, while enabling the following misunderstanding of 'pervert.' The English makes Taichi actively corrupt an already 'awful nature,' adding moral content and losing the intended transformation.

examples.japanese: 「おおう」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "CoOoOovEeEr... diIiIsguiIiIse..."
examples.note: The source contains only a sobbing exclamation. The English invents the words 'cover' and 'disguise' and a prolonged performance not present in the line.

examples.japanese: 美希がどの程度の戦力を持っているかを調べる。第一に設定されるシークエンスだ。
examples.ghs:
However, Miki's threat level is an unknown
variable, and therefore caution was required.
examples.note: The Japanese describes investigating the extent of Miki's fighting strength as the first planned sequence. The English replaces the investigation and ordering with a generic warning about caution.

examples.japanese: 「もうちょっと」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "Seriously, look at this now!"
examples.note: While holding Misato, Taichi says 'a little longer.' The English replaces that duration with an unrelated command to look at something.

examples.japanese: 左右や円などの動きをやめ、ただ行き帰るだけの運動に切り替える。
examples.ghs: I stop the motions left and right and circle, and in exchange, a motion that merely drives straight for home.
examples.note: The source says he stops lateral and circular movements and switches to simple back-and-forth strokes. “Drives straight for home” invents a destination idiom and omits the return motion.

dossiers.title: Concrete meaning is weakened into vagueness or euphemism
dossiers.claim: Specific objects, acts, or implications are repeatedly diluted into less informative English.
dossiers.sourcePattern: Japanese wording that makes a concrete referent, action, or force explicit.
dossiers.georgeHenryShaftEffect: The English suppresses the specificity that carries the line's point, tone, or payoff.
dossiers.limits: Natural compression is accepted when the same information and force remain recoverable.
dossiers.diagnostic: 452 confirmed findings: 8 critical, 98 major, 221 moderate, 125 minor.

examples.japanese: 「今日はみんなに、柿の種の教訓を話したいと思う」
examples.ghs: Sakuraba: "Today, I would like to hold a lesson with everyone regarding the Kaki, or Japanese persimmon."
examples.note: 柿の種 is the named rice-cracker snack and the lesson concerns it. The English misreads it as a lesson about persimmons themselves.

examples.japanese: 「こんなとき美希ちんだったら、ぺろぺろと舐めて癒してくれるのに」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "If it was Miki-chan in this situation, you'll be healing her by going all licky-licky with your tongue wouldn't you!"
examples.note: Taichi says that if Miki were here, she would lick his wound better. The English leaves the nickname suffix unexplained and instead says Kiri will heal Miki, reversing healer and patient.

examples.japanese: 先輩を信じるのだ。
examples.ghs: Senpai believes it.
examples.note: The narrator exhorts himself to trust his senior. The English instead makes the senior the person who believes something and leaves the title untranslated.

examples.japanese: 缶は飛ばない。誰かが投げた。誰が？　今考える必要はない。投げる。意図。意図を持って投げた。目的は？　缶を投げることによって期待できる効果。投げた缶が効果を発揮。
examples.ghs: Cans do not fly. Somebody threw it.
examples.note: After noting that cans do not fly and someone threw them, the Japanese continues through a rapid chain of questions about actor, intent, purpose, and expected effect. The English omits nearly the entire unit.

examples.japanese: 「会ったこともない処女に馴れ馴れしく話しかけられればな」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "When got close and talked to in a familiarly familiar way by a maiden whom I had no previous meets with."
examples.note: The source says anyone would pry when an unfamiliar virgin speaks to him with undue familiarity. The English is syntactically broken, euphemizes 処女 as 'maiden,' and uses the nonexistent phrase 'previous meets.'

examples.japanese: 「世界は人を塗りつぶした。俺たちだけが、『互い』だ」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "This world has painted out all people. We alone are... reciprocal."
examples.note: 俺たちだけが『互い』だ says that the survivors are now one another's only others or counterparts. 'We alone are reciprocal' is not idiomatic and fails to communicate that human relation.

examples.japanese: 「最高に姉貴と関係ない質問だよ！！」
examples.ghs: Tomoki: "That's the single most unrelated question to Aneki!!!"
examples.note: 姉貴 means the speaker's older sister, but 'Aneki' is left untranslated. 'Unrelated question to' is also the wrong English preposition.

examples.japanese: 人類は滅亡していた。
examples.ghs: Mankind had fallen.
examples.note: 滅亡していた states that humanity had become extinct. "Had fallen" can mean defeat or decline and does not communicate extinction.

dossiers.title: An inference is promoted into stated fact
dossiers.claim: The English repeatedly resolves implications more narrowly than the Japanese warrants.
dossiers.sourcePattern: Elliptical, suggestive, or underspecified wording whose local evidence supports more than one reading.
dossiers.georgeHenryShaftEffect: A possible interpretation becomes the narrator's or character's explicit assertion.
dossiers.limits: Contextually required completion is not included; only avoidable narrowing is counted.
dossiers.diagnostic: 200 confirmed findings: 3 critical, 52 major, 110 moderate, 35 minor.

examples.japanese: 「柿の種にピーナッツ入っているものがある。知っているな」
examples.ghs: Sakuraba: "There is a type of seed of persimmon, or Kaki no Tane, that is actually a peanut-based snack usually served with beer. Did you know?"
examples.note: Sakuraba says some versions of the kaki no tane snack contain peanuts and asks whether they know that. The English describes a persimmon seed as a peanut-based snack and adds an unsolicited serving custom.

examples.japanese: 霧の言葉が、切り裂いた。
examples.ghs: Kiri's words tore me to shreds.
examples.note: Kiri's next words cut through the narrator's unfinished speech. 'Tore me to shreds' changes the object from his words to his person and greatly increases the force.

examples.japanese: 「普通、キミみたいな役割はもっと大人しい電波っぽい娘がやるものだろ！」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "Normally, roles like yours would be assigned to a much more docile Denpa-emitter of a crazy girl, definitely."
examples.note: The Japanese says the role normally belongs to a quieter, denpa-like girl. The English invents an emitter, explicitly declares her crazy, and adds 'definitely.'

examples.japanese: 「部活も頑張れ。仲間が死んでも頑張れ。大丈夫、来週には笑っていられっから」
examples.ghs: Nanaka: "Give it all on club, too. True Companions may die, but still give it all. You'll be all right, because next week you'll be all laughs."
examples.note: Nanaka urges him to persist with the club even if companions die and says he will be able to smile next week. The English turns the concessive event into a possibility, invents a capitalized class, and changes smiling into being an object of laughter.

examples.japanese: 「傷つけて楽しむため、あなたの目はいつも私たちに注がれている。それもひと思いにではなく、ゆっくりと時間をかけて嬲り尽くそうとしている」
examples.ghs: Kiri: "Your eyes are always focused on us, so that you can enjoy the hurting. And it's not something done instantly, you slowly take the time to perform that bullish sexual 'teasing' of yours all the way to the end."
examples.note: Kiri accuses him of slowly tormenting people to exhaustion. The English invents both a bovine quality and a specifically sexual form of teasing.

examples.japanese: 「はだけて」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "Strip."
examples.note: Taichi tells Kiri to uncover the injured shoulder. 'Strip' instructs her to remove her clothing generally and greatly broadens the command.

examples.japanese: 無意識に代名詞を切り替えて問う。
examples.ghs: An inquiry with an unconsciously inserted slur.
examples.note: The narrator notes unconsciously switching his second-person pronoun to the rough 貴様. The English turns that pronoun choice into an inserted slur and omits the actual switch.

examples.japanese: 強襲、郵便局。
examples.ghs: I go postal.
examples.note: 強襲、郵便局 jokingly frames the post office visit as a raid or assault. The English imports an unrelated idiom for workplace violence.

dossiers.title: Time, completion, or duration changes
dossiers.claim: Japanese tense and aspect are repeatedly rendered with the wrong temporal shape.
dossiers.sourcePattern: Forms that distinguish ongoing action, resulting state, repetition, completion, or temporal sequence.
dossiers.georgeHenryShaftEffect: The English changes whether something happened, was happening, had continued, or merely seemed imminent.
dossiers.limits: English tense is allowed to shift naturally when discourse time and event structure remain intact.
dossiers.diagnostic: 641 confirmed findings: 12 critical, 127 major, 324 moderate, 178 minor.

examples.japanese: 胸を張る。
examples.ghs: Puff that chest with pride!
examples.note: 胸を張る is the narrator's present action of throwing out his chest. 'Puff that chest with pride!' changes it into an imperative addressed to someone else.

examples.japanese: 「逃げてるんだよ。昔からそうだ」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "I want to run away from her. Been like that for a long time."
examples.note: Taichi says that she is running away and always has. The English makes Taichi the one who wants to run away from her.

examples.japanese: 「だって、どっちにしろ世界はもう終わりなんですから」
examples.ghs: Kiri: "Because either way the world has already ended."
examples.note: Kiri says that the world will end anyway. The English says that it has already ended.

examples.japanese: 一度、掃除の人夫として駆り出されたことがある。
examples.ghs:
Once, it happened that I was tossed out when I
was working as a cleaning man.
examples.note: Taichi was once pressed into service as cleaning labor. 'Was tossed out when I was working as a cleaning man' instead says that he was ejected or dismissed.

examples.japanese: 「おかげで蹴られたり嫌われたり大変だったぞ」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "It's gonna be a mess if there's rejection or hatred because of that."
examples.note: The speaker says that because of this he had a hard time being rejected or hated. The English turns it into a future hypothetical mess if rejection or hatred happens and obscures who suffers it.

examples.japanese: ＊してから＊したんだっけ？
examples.ghs: You're xxxxed, therefore you ****?
examples.note: The narrator asks whether one censored action happened after another and then questions the order. The English changes the person, tense, and relation into a general implication.

examples.japanese: 「ちょっと、この子が入ってくる頃には私たちいないんじゃないの？」
examples.ghs: Touko: "Hold it, when this girl came around none of us were there weren't we?"
examples.note: The source says that by the time this girl enters the school, they will no longer be there. The English changes that future absence into a past claim that they were not there when she arrived.

examples.japanese: 「はっ！？　まさか俺を、俺をその淫妖花弁の虜に堕落せしめた挙げ句に精髄をすすってダメにする気だな！？」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "Huh?! Could it be, could it be that I have been made to fall into captivity of this bawdy bewitching petal and that I will be made to spoil by having all my essences slurped out?!"
examples.note: The source accuses her of intending to ensnare him, then suck out his essence and ruin him. The English makes the captivity already completed, shifts the threat into passive future states, and is syntactically broken.

dossiers.title: The English is grammatically malformed
dossiers.claim: The translation repeatedly produces agreement, complementation, article, valency, or sentence-structure errors.
dossiers.sourcePattern: Japanese lines whose intended proposition is recoverable enough to judge the resulting English construction.
dossiers.georgeHenryShaftEffect: The sentence reads as broken or forces the reader to reconstruct basic syntax.
dossiers.limits: Deliberate fragments and character-specific disfluency are preserved when they function in context.
dossiers.diagnostic: 2,305 confirmed findings: 37 critical, 538 major, 739 moderate, 991 minor.

examples.japanese: 「……そんなわけ」
examples.ghs: Tomoki: "...that'd be, well."
examples.note: そんなわけ is the beginning of a denial such as 'No way' before the line trails off. 'That'd be, well' is neither grammatical nor a denial.

examples.japanese: 後に美希と知り合った霧は、二人そろって放送部に入ることになった。
examples.ghs: Having subsequently been acquainted with Miki, it became that her and Kiri came to the Broadcast Club together.
examples.note: Kiri later became acquainted with Miki, and the two joined the club together. The English's participial clause has no subject, then treats 'her' and Kiri as two separate people and uses an object pronoun as subject.

examples.japanese: 「これが俺のアイデンティティなんだよ。他の接し方はない」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "This is my eye-dentity indeed. Other ways to deal with things I haven't."
examples.note: アイデンティティ is simply the loanword 'identity.' The English invents an 'eye-dentity' pun absent from the source, then leaves the following sentence in non-English object-first order.

examples.japanese: 「ちょ、やだ、やだやだやだやだっ、やだーーーーーーーーーーっ！」
examples.ghs: Kiri: "Wa, you don't, don'tdon'tdon'tdon't, you dooooOOOOOON'T!"
examples.note: Kiri repeatedly says that she does not want this. The English changes her first-person refusal into an incoherent second-person statement.

examples.japanese: ガラス細工の霧もまた、砕ける一瞬がもっとも。
examples.ghs: Even more for the glasswork that is Kiri, that like it would pulverize in an instant. Appropriate.
examples.note: The thought says that for glasswork Kiri too, the instant when she shatters is the most—, trailing into the next line. The English is ungrammatical and substitutes 'appropriate' for the superlative もっとも.

examples.japanese: 万が一に俺が忘れたとしても……曜子ちゃんなら自力で真実までたどり着くだろう。
examples.ghs: Thousand will give you one that I even if I forget... Youko-chan can eventually reach the truth on her own power alone, definitely.
examples.note: The Japanese says that even in the unlikely event that the narrator forgets, Youko can reach the truth herself. The English is grammatically incoherent and fails to convey the conditional.

examples.japanese: どうしてカメラを、持ってこなかったんだ……俺は？
examples.ghs: How come a camera you didn't bring with... myself?
examples.note: The narrator asks himself why he did not bring a camera. The English shifts to second person, strands the object, and appends a contradictory reflexive.

examples.japanese: 「そうです。何も起こらなければ、ここは……」
examples.ghs: Misato: "Right then. If nothing goes wrong, because us being here..."
examples.note: The Japanese begins a conditional statement that if nothing had happened, this place or project would have proceeded. The English inserts 'because,' uses an object pronoun as a subject, and fails to convey the clause.

dossiers.title: Dictionary-near words fail in context
dossiers.claim: Lexically related English choices repeatedly carry the wrong sense, collocation, or interpersonal force.
dossiers.sourcePattern: A Japanese word or phrase whose local sense is constrained by its construction and scene context.
dossiers.georgeHenryShaftEffect: The English may remain superficially plausible while sounding wrong or meaning the wrong thing.
dossiers.limits: Stylistic alternatives are not findings unless the selected word creates a semantic or idiomatic failure.
dossiers.diagnostic: 1,528 confirmed findings: 12 critical, 337 major, 698 moderate, 481 minor.

examples.japanese: このガキ、空気を読むということをしないのか。
examples.ghs: Can't this ghoul of a brat just not read the mood?
examples.note: Taichi asks whether the brat cannot read the room. The English adds 'ghoul' and its double negative instead asks whether he can refrain from reading it.

examples.japanese: 「いっそ楽にしてくれよ～っと♪」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "Please release me from my pleee～asure!♪"
examples.note: 楽にしてくれ asks to be put out of his misery or relieved of suffering. The English chooses 'pleasure,' reversing pain relief into release from enjoyment.

examples.japanese: 処女貫通悶絶二穴責めから解放されたのは、十分後だった。
examples.ghs: I was freed from the swooningly agonizing Dual Hole Virginity Piercing torture an adequate ten minutes later.
examples.note: 十分後 means ten minutes later. The English misreads the homograph 十分 as the adjective 'adequate' and attaches that unrelated sense to the duration.

examples.japanese: キレた霧に蹴倒された。
examples.ghs: Kiboshlessly kickdowned by Kiri.
examples.note: The phrase uses a nonexistent adverb and a nonexistent past participle, and it omits that Kiri had snapped before kicking Taichi down.

examples.japanese: たまに覚醒してしまう者もいたが。
examples.ghs:
Occasionally, there were people who grew
disillusioned, but,
examples.note: 覚醒 means that some participants awakened to or discovered a new appetite. 'Grew disillusioned' means they lost belief or enthusiasm, the opposite direction.

examples.japanese: 「いちおう部員なんだし、何か言えこのスベタ」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "As far as it goes you're a club member, aren't you, so say something you curtana!"
examples.note: スベタ is a derogatory term for a woman, such as “shrew.” “Curtana” is the name of a ceremonial sword and is unrelated.

examples.japanese: 「会ったこともない処女に馴れ馴れしく話しかけられればな」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "When got close and talked to in a familiarly familiar way by a maiden whom I had no previous meets with."
examples.note: The source says anyone would pry when an unfamiliar virgin speaks to him with undue familiarity. The English is syntactically broken, euphemizes 処女 as 'maiden,' and uses the nonexistent phrase 'previous meets.'

examples.japanese: 「世界は人を塗りつぶした。俺たちだけが、『互い』だ」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "This world has painted out all people. We alone are... reciprocal."
examples.note: 俺たちだけが『互い』だ says that the survivors are now one another's only others or counterparts. 'We alone are reciprocal' is not idiomatic and fails to communicate that human relation.

dossiers.title: Japanese phrasing is copied into non-English idiom
dossiers.claim: Source constructions are repeatedly transferred word by word instead of rebuilt as functioning English.
dossiers.sourcePattern: Conventional Japanese phrasing whose communicative value has a normal English realization.
dossiers.georgeHenryShaftEffect: The result is stiff, opaque, or accidentally comic even when individual words are recognizable.
dossiers.limits: Authorial fragmentation and deliberate strangeness are not normalized merely for smoothness.
dossiers.diagnostic: 953 confirmed findings: 7 critical, 203 major, 371 moderate, 372 minor.

examples.japanese: 部屋の生ぬるさが戻り、じんわりと身を包む。
examples.ghs: The room returning to half-hearted lukewarmth, I begin to dress myself.
examples.note: The lukewarm air of the room returns and gently envelops his body. The English calls the warmth 'half-hearted' and changes the room's enveloping action into Taichi beginning to dress himself.

examples.japanese: 「だめ。彼女は自分を持ってない」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "Not happening. She can't hold herself down."
examples.note: 自分を持ってない means that she has no self or identity of her own. 'Can't hold herself down' instead describes failed restraint.

examples.japanese: 役不足もいいところだ。
examples.ghs: At best it could be said to be the dissatisfaction with one's lot in life.
examples.note: In context, 役不足もいいところ says that his reason is utterly unequal to its assigned task. The English gives an unrelated dictionary-like notion of dissatisfaction with one's lot.

examples.japanese: ギロッという感じの視線が、俺を射竦める。
examples.ghs: The feeling of a sight using me as a guiro, pinning me down.
examples.note: ギロッ is the mimetic force of a sharp glare. The English mistakes it for the musical instrument 'guiro' and consequently destroys the sentence's action.

examples.japanese: 「精神より先に体が根を上げる」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "The roots of the body are easier to extirpate than the mind's."
examples.note: 体が音を上げる means the body will give out or cry uncle before the mind does. The English invents bodily roots being extirpated and loses the mind-body endurance contrast.

examples.japanese: つうかモロ見えてるし。
examples.ghs: But very much all of her frankness is visible.
examples.note: モロ見えてる says the intimate view is fully and plainly exposed. 'All of her frankness is visible' mistakes モロ for emotional candor and removes the physical meaning.

examples.japanese: 座った目で言う。
examples.ghs: She says, with eyes that look like they've been through glasses.
examples.note: The source describes fixed, glazed, or dead-serious eyes. The English invents eyes that have physically passed through spectacles and does not convey her stare.

examples.japanese: 「まーまー、待ちたまえよ。ロマンは一日にして成らずだ」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "Waiiit, waiiit, gladden me with holding on! Romance wasn't built in a day!"
examples.note: 待ちたまえ means 'wait' or 'hold on.' 'Gladden me with holding on' is an unrelated and unidiomatic command that breaks the Rome/romance proverb joke.

dossiers.title: The written presentation obscures the intended line
dossiers.claim: Line construction, segmentation, or surface presentation repeatedly makes otherwise recoverable content harder to read.
dossiers.sourcePattern: A source unit whose divisions, repetitions, or emphasis contribute to its delivery.
dossiers.georgeHenryShaftEffect: The English introduces distracting breaks, malformed sequencing, or an incoherent visual sentence.
dossiers.limits: Engine line breaks and deliberate repetitions are retained when they carry timing or voice.
dossiers.diagnostic: 450 confirmed findings: 19 critical, 95 major, 119 moderate, 217 minor.

examples.japanese: 「あー、太一！　あんたいったいどういうつもりで約束すっぽかして……」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "Ahhh, Taichi! What the devil do you think you are doing, making arrangements and then standing people up..."
examples.note: The Japanese line is Touko angrily addressing Taichi. The English assigns the line to Taichi, making him complain to himself.

examples.japanese: 「しようとしたけど、きついこと言われて引き下がった」
examples.ghs: Miki: "You were going to, but you were told something harsh and were stopped."
examples.note: Taichi admits in the first person that he tried but backed down after being told something harsh. The English labels Miki as speaker and changes the confession into her second-person account of his behavior.

examples.japanese: 「違います！」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "Not like that!"
examples.note: Misato protests 'That's not what I mean' after clutching her chest. The English labels Taichi as the speaker, reversing the dialogue role.

examples.japanese: 「師匠と弟子っすから」
examples.ghs: Misato: "We are teacher and pupil, that is why."
examples.note: The authoritative source identifies Miki as the speaker. The English labels the line as Misato's, reversing the dialogue role.

examples.japanese: 「……おそろしい……世の中どうかしてる……」
examples.ghs:
Touko: "Can't be! That absolutely can't be!"
Misato: "Hyeee～h, beauty and the beee～ast!"
Tomoki: "...terrifying... the world's gone mad..."
examples.note: This source unit contains only one short reaction about the frightening state of the world. The English prepends two additional characters’ lines that are not bound to this source span.

examples.japanese: 「ＹＥＳ、ＢＯＳＳ」
examples.ghs:
Taichi: "HAI, BUCHOU!"
/screw it *chug* -GHS
examples.note: The source is already English: “YES, BOSS.” The translation replaces it with Japanese “HAI, BUCHOU” and appends an unbound translator aside.

examples.japanese: 「この酸いも甘いも噛みしめたヤングアダルト候補生、黒須太一の目をごまかしたくば、気の利いたパンチラ嬢の一人でも連れてくるんだな！」
examples.ghs: This is an elite cadet of young adulthood who is experienced in the ways of the world, having tasted both its bitter and its sweet! To deceive the eyes of Kurosu Taichi is something a clever Panchira-jou alone will never accomplish!"
examples.note: The source boasts that if she wants to fool Kurosu Taichi, she should bring at least one quick-witted panty-flash girl. The English lacks its opening quote and reverses the challenge into a claim that such a girl alone could never succeed.

examples.japanese: 「……必要ない」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "...unneeded."
examples.note: The Japanese speaker metadata identifies Tōko as the speaker of '...No need.' The English labels the line as Taichi, assigning the reply to the wrong character.

dossiers.title: Punctuation and typography change the reading
dossiers.claim: Mechanical marks repeatedly damage syntax, quotation, emphasis, or legibility.
dossiers.sourcePattern: A line whose punctuation or typographic treatment can be separated from interpretive translation choices.
dossiers.georgeHenryShaftEffect: The English becomes ambiguous, malformed, or visibly unfinished.
dossiers.limits: House-style variation is not counted unless it changes sense or produces an objective error.
dossiers.diagnostic: 188 confirmed findings: 1 critical, 19 major, 24 moderate, 144 minor.

examples.japanese: 「けどちょっと甘くしたらベタってしすぎるよ！　水気が多すぎだよ！　もっと徹底して勝ち気っぽく行こうよ！　照れる時は厳選。その方が萌え……桐原のためなんだ」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "But if you get this sweet, you'll also be far too hackneyed! There's too much dampness! Let's be more consistently unyielding! Select carefully when to show shyness. Someone like that is moe... be that, Kirihara!
examples.note: ベタベタ means overly clingy or syrupy, not hackneyed, and the extended character-direction monologue culminates in a lie that this is for Kirihara's sake. The English becomes incoherent at 'Someone like that is moe... be that,' omits that pivot, and lacks a closing quotation mark.

examples.japanese: 「部活も頑張れ。仲間が死んでも頑張れ。大丈夫、来週には笑っていられっから」
examples.ghs: Nanaka: "Give it all on club, too. True Companions may die, but still give it all. You'll be all right, because next week you'll be all laughs."
examples.note: Nanaka urges him to persist with the club even if companions die and says he will be able to smile next week. The English turns the concessive event into a possibility, invents a capitalized class, and changes smiling into being an object of laughter.

examples.japanese: 「パラシュート・デス・センテンスを成立させるための時間は、わずか０．０５秒に過ぎない。ではここで、そのプロセスをもう一度見てみることに―――」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "To bring a Parachute Death Sentence into existence, the time taken is a mere 0.05" and no more. Therefore, let us now see the process for ourselves one more t---"
examples.note: The Japanese gives 0.05 seconds. The English replaces the unit with a stray closing quotation mark and adds 'and no more.'

examples.japanese: 外障だと思っていた。
examples.ghs: I had thought he was External Damage.
examples.note: 外障 abbreviates an external disability. 'Damage' describes injury to an object, not a person's disability, and the capitalization invents an official category name.

examples.japanese: 可愛い血の繋がらない妹的存在と暮らしている。
examples.ghs: He is living together with a Cute Non-Blood Related Imouto-like being.
examples.note: The Japanese describes living with a cute, unrelated, little-sister-like figure. The English leaves imouto untranslated, capitalizes the entire description, and dehumanizes her as a 'being.'

examples.japanese: 発展性のない世界にあるのは、可能性という娯楽だけ。
examples.ghs:
A world in which advancement has no
consequence is a world that only has the
the amusement of the potential.
examples.note: 発展性のない世界 is a world with no potential for development, in which possibility itself is the only amusement. The English instead says advancement has no consequence, duplicates 'the,' and preserves intrusive engine line breaks.

examples.japanese: ズボンとパンツは。
examples.ghs: Trousers and undies where...
examples.note: The sentence fragment is missing its predicate, and 'where' is a spelling error for 'were.'

examples.japanese: 「あ、桐原せむぱいはどうでした？」
examples.ghs: Miki: "Ah, how wHas Kirihara-semhpai?"
examples.note: The English question is corrupted by the string 'how wHas' and the speaker-title string is also misspelled.

dossiers.title: Names and forms of address are unstable
dossiers.claim: Names, titles, honorific relations, and direct address are repeatedly mistranscribed, substituted, or inconsistently projected.
dossiers.sourcePattern: Explicit names and address forms, together with stable speaker and relationship context.
dossiers.georgeHenryShaftEffect: Identity or interpersonal stance changes, sometimes within the same recurring form.
dossiers.limits: Defensible localization choices are accepted when identity and relationship remain stable.
dossiers.diagnostic: 788 confirmed findings: 13 critical, 57 major, 74 moderate, 644 minor.

examples.japanese: 『姪がさー、やっぱ群青行くんだけどさ、いろいろ教えてやらんと』
examples.ghs: Shinkawa: 『Got a niece, ya know, 'course she goes to Gunjou, ya know, so she's telling me lots and lots of stuff.』
examples.note: Shinkawa says his niece will also attend Gunjō and that he needs to teach her various things. The English says she already attends and reverses the teaching direction so that she tells him things.

examples.japanese: 「こんなとき美希ちんだったら、ぺろぺろと舐めて癒してくれるのに」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "If it was Miki-chan in this situation, you'll be healing her by going all licky-licky with your tongue wouldn't you!"
examples.note: Taichi says that if Miki were here, she would lick his wound better. The English leaves the nickname suffix unexplained and instead says Kiri will heal Miki, reversing healer and patient.

examples.japanese: 先輩を信じるのだ。
examples.ghs: Senpai believes it.
examples.note: The narrator exhorts himself to trust his senior. The English instead makes the senior the person who believes something and leaves the title untranslated.

examples.japanese: 「中原好きなんです」
examples.ghs: Misato: "So you like Nakahara it seems."
examples.note: Misato says that she likes Nakahara Chūya. The English assigns that preference to Taichi and does not normalize the name to standard Hepburn.

examples.japanese: ちょっと龍馬入ってる。
examples.ghs: There's also a bit of the war horse, gallant in the face of battle.
examples.note: 龍馬 refers to Ryoma and explains Taichi's imitation of the distinctive ぜよ speech. The English translates the name's characters as a generic 'war horse' and invents a battle description.

examples.japanese: 群青の冬子は一人だった。
examples.ghs: Touko the Ultramarine of Gunjou was alone.
examples.note: 群青 is the institution or group name Gunjou in this construction. 'Touko the Ultramarine of Gunjou' translates the same name twice and invents an epithet.

examples.japanese: 先輩と美希がいた。
examples.ghs: Senpai and Kiri were there.
examples.note: The Japanese says that Senpai and Miki were there. The English substitutes Kiri for Miki.

examples.japanese: 「貴様、地球人ではないな？」
examples.ghs: Nanaka: "You bastard, you're not an earthling are you?"
examples.note: The source speaker is Taichi accusing Nanaka of not being an earthling. The English label assigns Taichi's line to Nanaka, making her accuse him instead.

dossiers.title: Register and character voice shift without support
dossiers.claim: The English repeatedly changes politeness, aggression, intimacy, age, or social posture beyond what the Japanese line supports.
dossiers.sourcePattern: Lexis, endings, address, and surrounding voice evidence that constrain the line's interpersonal register.
dossiers.georgeHenryShaftEffect: A speaker can become harsher, flatter, more formal, or more evasive than in the source.
dossiers.limits: Natural English need not imitate Japanese surface politeness; the tested quantity is the resulting relationship and force.
dossiers.diagnostic: 569 confirmed findings: 8 critical, 115 major, 257 moderate, 189 minor.

examples.japanese: 「させるか！」
examples.ghs: Miki: "'Cause I'll let ya!"
examples.note: させるか means 'Like hell I'll let you!' The English says the exact opposite—that she will allow it—and adds an unsupported causal fragment.

examples.japanese: 「めっちゃニヤけてるんですけど」
examples.ghs: Miki: "But you're totally an effeminate fop with a catty grin."
examples.note: Miki simply points out that he is grinning broadly. The English invents gendered and class-coded insults and attributes cattiness absent from the source.

examples.japanese: 「いけね」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "Cut it out now."
examples.note: いけね is Taichi's realization, 'Oops' or 'Oh, right.' The English turns it into a command directed at someone else.

examples.japanese: 「おおう」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "CoOoOovEeEr... diIiIsguiIiIse..."
examples.note: The source contains only a sobbing exclamation. The English invents the words 'cover' and 'disguise' and a prolonged performance not present in the line.

examples.japanese: 「もきーっ、あの小娘ーっ」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "MokYYYYY, that puss!!!"
examples.note: 小娘 is “little brat/girl.” “Puss” is a sexualized English insult with different connotations and force.

examples.japanese: 「ぎゃふんっ」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "Mine is the silence of agreement."
examples.note: ぎゃふん is a comic cry of defeat or being silenced. 'Mine is the silence of agreement' replaces the utterance with a formal abstract declaration.

examples.japanese: つんつんと指先を見合わせる。
examples.ghs: My fingertips bounce off of each other in the manner of someone aloof and easily irritated.
examples.note: The source shows the speaker touching her index fingertips together in a bashful gesture. The English invents aloofness and irritability, assigning the gesture the opposite social affect.

examples.japanese: 「黒須太一は特に動くな！」
examples.ghs: Kiri: "Kurosu Taichi in particular will not move!"
examples.note: The source is a forceful imperative directed especially at Kurosu Taichi. 'Will not move' changes the command into an awkward future declaration.

dossiers.title: Jokes and wordplay lose their working mechanism
dossiers.claim: The translation repeatedly preserves stray words while dropping the ambiguity, repetition, or setup that makes the exchange function.
dossiers.sourcePattern: A recoverable pun, lexical echo, mishearing, or deliberate double reading in its surrounding exchange.
dossiers.georgeHenryShaftEffect: The English keeps the shell of the line but removes the reason it is funny or consequential.
dossiers.limits: Functional rewrites are acceptable; the English does not need to reproduce the Japanese mechanism literally.
dossiers.diagnostic: 165 confirmed findings: 21 critical, 80 major, 60 moderate, 4 minor.

examples.japanese: 「オレを素に戻らせたおまえの引かせパワー、許し難い」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "Your Pulling Power caused me to return to unembellishment, irremissible!"
examples.note: Taichi condemns Sakuraba's power to make him recoil and snap out of his performance. The English misreads 引かせ as physical pulling, literalizes 素 as lack of embellishment, and ends with a dangling adjective.

examples.japanese: これは耳拷問、無意味に略せばみみごーではないか。
examples.ghs: this is Ear Torture, or if one wants to nonsensically abbreviate it, ExtraTerrestrial.
examples.note: The narrator nonsensically abbreviates 耳拷問, 'ear torture,' as みみごー to set up the following sound play. 'Extraterrestrial' has no relation to either component and replaces the joke with unrelated content.

examples.japanese: 「これが俺のアイデンティティなんだよ。他の接し方はない」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "This is my eye-dentity indeed. Other ways to deal with things I haven't."
examples.note: アイデンティティ is simply the loanword 'identity.' The English invents an 'eye-dentity' pun absent from the source, then leaves the following sentence in non-English object-first order.

examples.japanese: 「そしていずれは、酸いも甘いも噛み分けたヤングアダルトへと変態していくのです」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "And then shall I, at last, pervert my awful nature into that of a Young Adult that is experienced in the ways of the world, having tasted its bitter and its sweet!"
examples.note: 変態する means transform or metamorphose, while enabling the following misunderstanding of 'pervert.' The English makes Taichi actively corrupt an already 'awful nature,' adding moral content and losing the intended transformation.

examples.japanese: ちょっと龍馬入ってる。
examples.ghs: There's also a bit of the war horse, gallant in the face of battle.
examples.note: 龍馬 refers to Ryoma and explains Taichi's imitation of the distinctive ぜよ speech. The English translates the name's characters as a generic 'war horse' and invents a battle description.

examples.japanese: 「友貴もどうだ、姉弟ネコイラズで」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "But you're doing this too, Tomoki, if I may meddle in the poisoning of siblings."
examples.note: Taichi invites Tomoki to join, making a malapropism that substitutes 'rat poison' for the idiom meaning family together without outsiders. The English invents meddling in sibling poisoning and says Tomoki already participates.

examples.japanese: 「てんそ（天然素材）なんだって」
examples.ghs: Tomoki: "Natural Raw (Natural airhead as Raw materials) innhe."
examples.note: The source explains the clipped pun てんそ as 天然素材, “natural material,” while also invoking an airhead. “Natural Raw ... as Raw materials” is ungrammatical and fails to preserve either phrase cleanly.

examples.japanese: 「そのピティワードに免じて見逃してやりたいところだが、どこの星から来たのかくらい白状していけ！」
examples.ghs: Taichi: "If you do desire me to deferentially overlook that pitiful affectation of a word, then confess at least from which star you come from!"
examples.note: ピティワード continues the 'pretty word' joke, not a pitiful affectation. The source says he would like to let her off in consideration of it but demands a confession; the English turns that into a condition about what she desires and also duplicates 'from.'
